segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his slaves what must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his slave John,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who testified to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, to all that he saw.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of the prophecy, and blessed are those who hear them and keep what is written in it, for the time is near.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John, to the seven assemblies in Asia: Grace to you and peace from the one who is and who was and who is coming, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth. To him who loves us and freed us from our sins by his blood—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father—to him be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. Yes, amen.

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “I am the Alpha and the Omega,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: says the Lord God,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “the one who is and who was and who is coming, the Almighty.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I, John, your brother and partner in the affliction and kingdom and endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Write what you see on a scroll and send it to the seven assemblies: to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me, and when I turned I saw seven golden lampstands,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and in the midst of the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed in a robe reaching to his feet and with a golden sash wrapped around his chest.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His head and his hair were white like white wool, like snow, and his eyes were like a flame of fire,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and his feet were like fine bronze when it has been fired in a furnace, and his voice was like the sound of many waters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had seven stars in his right hand, and from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in its strength.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. And he laid his right hand on me, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the living one. I was dead, and look, I am alive forever and ever, and I have the keys of death and of Hades.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Write, then, what you have seen, and what is, and what is going to take place after this.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As for the mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies, and the seven lampstands are the seven assemblies.”

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master. The Septuagint uses it for Moses and the prophets as God’s own, so here it is a title of honour as well as of belonging. Most English versions soften it to “servants”, which loses the note of ownership a first-century reader would have heard.

The Greek has one reader and many hearers. The scene is a gathering in which one person reads the book aloud to the rest, which was the normal way a text reached most people. The blessing falls on that public reader and on the listening community.

The word meant a gathering of citizens, and in the Septuagint it is the term for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is well understood, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

notes.phrase: the one who is and who was and who is coming
notes.traditional: him who is and who was and who is to come
notes.note: The phrase echoes God’s self-naming in the Greek version of Exodus 3:14, “I am the one who is.” John leaves it grammatically uninflected after a preposition that would normally change its form. This is generally taken as deliberate, treating the phrase as an unchangeable name. The last element is literally “the coming one”, not simply “who will be”.

Many interpreters take this as a symbolic description of the one Spirit of God in its fullness, since it stands between God and Jesus Christ in the greeting. Others take it as seven principal angels who stand before God’s throne. The lower-case plural leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

The earliest manuscripts read “freed” (or “loosed”). Many later manuscripts read “washed”, which in Greek differs by a single letter and sounded almost the same. Modern editions and most modern translations follow the earlier reading.

notes.phrase: all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him
notes.traditional: all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him
notes.note: The verse weaves together Daniel 7:13 (one coming with the clouds) and Zechariah 12:10 (they look on the one they pierced and mourn). The Greek word for “earth” can also mean “land”, and in Zechariah the mourners are the clans of the land of Israel. Most interpreters think John has widened the scope to all peoples.

The Greek word is an everyday term for distress, pressure or hardship. “Tribulation” is the traditional rendering, but it has become a technical term for an end-time period, which the word does not in itself imply. Some modern versions use “suffering” or “persecution”.

This is the earliest known occurrence of the phrase. Most scholars take it to mean the first day of the week, Sunday, as Christian writers of the following generations use it. A minority read it as the prophetic “day of the Lord”, but that is a different expression in Greek.

The text does not name the owner of the trumpet-like voice. It is attributed here to Jesus because John turns to see the voice and sees the figure of verses 13–18, who repeats the command to write in verse 19. Some interpreters think the first voice belongs to an angel.

notes.phrase: one like a son of man
notes.traditional: one like the Son of Man
notes.note: The wording comes from Daniel 7:13, where “a son of man” is a Semitic way of saying a human being, so the phrase means a figure of human appearance. The Greek has no article, so it is not quite the Gospel title “the Son of Man”, though readers would have made the connection. Translations are divided between the two forms.

The Greek word is found only in Revelation (here and 2:18) and in writings that depend on it, so its exact meaning is uncertain. It is clearly a copper alloy of high quality, and guesses include a refined bronze or a brass. The picture of gleaming metal is clear even though the metallurgy is not.

notes.phrase: what you have seen, and what is, and what is going to take place after this
notes.traditional: the things that you have seen, those that are and those that are to take place after this
notes.note: This can be read as three items (the vision just seen, the present situation, the future), and some take it as an outline of the book. It can also be read as two: “what you have seen, both what is and what is going to take place.” The translation keeps the Greek order and lets either reading stand.

The Greek word means “messenger” and can be used of a human envoy or of a heavenly being. Everywhere else in Revelation it refers to heavenly beings, so most scholars understand a heavenly representative or guardian of each community. Others take these to be human messengers or leaders of the assemblies.

candidates.reason: Translators split between “slave”, “servant” and “bond-servant”, and the word recurs across every part of the New Testament, both literally and as a title for believers and apostles.
It varies between “tribulation”, “affliction”, “suffering”, “distress” and “persecution”, and “tribulation” carries end-times baggage that matters especially in Revelation and Matthew 24.
It recurs in the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, where “mystery” suggests a puzzle and the period sense is a secret now disclosed; one decision is needed between “mystery” and “secret”.

candidates.rendering: forever and ever (in εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων)
candidates.reason: The doxology formula and the word’s other uses (“age”, “world”, “forever”) recur throughout the New Testament and need a consistent policy on idiom versus literal “ages”.
It varies between “patience”, “perseverance”, “endurance” and “steadfastness” across the letters and Revelation, and readers should see it is one word.
